docs.title: maestro
docs.text:
Python helpers for orchestrating embedded Linux and FPGA workflows, especially AMD ZynqMP / Kria projects that combine Git, Bender, embgen, Vitis, Vivado/HoG, Apptainer, and Yocto.

Maestro is a library with a generated CLI. Workflow scripts import command wrappers, compose them in Python, and get consistent subprocess execution, logging, path handling, and configuration. The same wrappers are available from the shell as maestro <tool> <method>.

docs.title: What is included
docs.text:
• Command wrappers for git, bender, embgen, vitis / Vivado, CERN HoG, Verible, Yocto, and disk flashing (bmaptool)
  • Executors for host shells, uv run, Docker, and Apptainer containers, selectable per command in maestro.yml
  • A maestro CLI generated from the command wrappers (aliases meastro, mao)
  • Built-in Vitis helper scripts for RPU firmware setup, application creation, and builds
  • A built-in Apptainer definition for Yocto workflows
  • Shared configuration from maestro.yml and maestro.local.yml
  • Rich console logging plus per-run log files under .maestro/runs/

docs.title: Who this is for
docs.text: Engineers who already run ZynqMP toolchains and want Python scripts that clone repos, generate registers, build FPGA bitstreams, compile RPU firmware, and bake Yocto images without reinventing subprocess and logging plumbing each time.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Getting started - install and run a minimal script
  • CLI - run any wrapper from the shell
  • Architecture - how commands, executors, and config fit together
  • Executors - run commands on the host or in containers
  • Guides - registers, Vivado/HoG, RPU firmware, Yocto
  • API reference - generated from the package

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
Every command wrapper is also reachable from the shell. The CLI is generated from the *Commands classes in maestro.commands: their signatures become the flags, and their Google-style docstrings become the --help text.

uv run maestro --help

meastro and mao are aliases for maestro.

docs.title: Command shape
docs.text:
maestro [--cwd DIR] <tool> [constructor flags] <method> [method flags] [positionals]
Python CLI GitCommands maestro git GitCommands.sha(short=True) maestro git sha --short HoGCommands.workflow("vivado/abacus", recreate=True) maestro hog workflow vivado/abacus --recreate GitCommands.clone(url, "out") maestro git clone URL out or maestro git clone --repo-url URL --dest out YoctoCommands("yocto/2025.2").bitbake("petalinux-image-minimal") maestro yocto --yocto-workdir yocto/2025.2 bitbake petalinux-image-minimal CommandConfig(cwd=DIR) --cwd DIR (before the tool)

Mapping rules:

  • Method and argument names: snake_case becomes kebab-case (submodule_update -> submodule-update, --repo-url)
  • Every parameter is a flag. Parameters without a default are required.
  • Required method parameters can also be given by position, in signature order. Flags and positional values can be combined, but positional values must stay together (clone URL --dest out works, clone URL --checkout main out does not). A list takes every value the required parameters after it don't need. Put -- before values that start with -.
  • Constructor parameters and required values that are not strings, paths or lists of them stay flags.
  • bool parameters become --x / --no-x
  • list[...] parameters accept several values (maestro verible format --patterns 'rtl/*.sv' 'tb/*.sv')
  • *args parameters take the positional values left over.
  • Path parameters are converted. str | Path stays a string.
  • A parameter named help is exposed as --show-help
  • Constructor parameters such as --executor-id go between the tool and the method

docs.title: Output and exit codes
docs.text:
• Logs go to stderr, and command output is streamed there as well
  • Return values go to stdout, so the CLI pipes cleanly: maestro git sha --short > rev.txt. Lists are printed one item per line, and sets are sorted first.
  • A method that returns a CommandResult exits with its return code
  • Any exception is logged as one line, exits with 1, and the traceback goes to the run's maestro.log

Executors come from maestro.yml (see Executors), so the same CLI call can run on the host or in a container without code changes.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Requirements: Python >= 3.11 and uv.

uv sync --all-extras

docs.title: Development commands
docs.text:
make format      # ruff format
make check       # ruff check --fix
make typecheck   # ty check
make pre-commit  # prek hooks (REUSE, YAML/TOML checks, whitespace, ...)
make lint        # all of the above
make test        # pytest
make license     # add SPDX headers and run reuse lint

Or the underlying tools:

uv run ruff format
uv run ruff check --fix
uv run ty check
uv run prek run --all-files
uv run pytest

CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs on Linux with Python 3.12. It checks the lockfile, formatting, lint, types, and REUSE compliance, runs the tests, and builds the documentation. Test reports and the built documentation are available as workflow downloads. A GitLab CI template is available for downstream FPGA projects. Run make lint and make test before pushing.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• Linux is the reference platform. A few tests assume POSIX and fail on a Windows host; that is known, not a regression. On Windows, run the suite in WSL.
  • Every bug fix gets a test that fails without the fix.
  • Vendor tools (Vivado, Vitis, HoG, Bender, embgen, Docker, Apptainer) are not available in CI. Prefer real child processes with fake tools: a fake binary on PATH, printf "[%s]" to show argv, or a recording executor that returns a CommandResult.
  • Tests that call load_config(tmp_path) change global state.

docs.title: Code style
docs.text:
• Google-style docstrings with Args: and Returns:. The CLI builds --help from them, and the API reference is generated from them.
  • Comments explain why, not what.
  • Run commands through Commands.run, not self.executor.run, so logging and the wrapper's CommandConfig apply.
  • Pass argv as a list; never join arguments with spaces. A single string is a shell script.

docs.title: Commits and pull requests
docs.text:
• Commit subjects are imperative, sentence case, without a trailing period, e.g. Resolve Commands cwd once so per-call configs don't re-apply it.
  • One fix per commit.
  • Pull request descriptions have three parts: Summary (one subsection per change, with the user-visible effect), Tests (new tests and the Linux result), and Notes (limits, what was not run).

docs.title: AI-assisted contributions
docs.text: AI coding assistants are welcome. The rules above apply unchanged: you are responsible for what you submit, it must pass lint and tests, and bug fixes need a test that fails without the fix. Say in the pull request if a substantial part was generated. See Use of AI in the README.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
make docs_serve   # live preview
make docs_build   # static site under site/

Edit Markdown under docs/ and navigation in mkdocs.yml. API pages use mkdocstrings; prefer improving docstrings in src/maestro/ when the reference output is thin. When you change a signature, check docs/guides/ for examples that call it.

docs.title: License headers
docs.text:
Contributions are accepted under the project license, Apache-2.0.

Every file carries an SPDX header (REUSE is enforced by the prek hooks). make license adds headers to known paths and runs reuse lint. When you add a file, add yourself as SPDX-FileContributor, and add your name to the "Authors and contributors" list in the README. Files that cannot carry a header (README.md, uv.lock, images) are covered in REUSE.toml.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.11+
  • uv for install and development

Tooling used by the workflow guides (install what your workflow needs):

  • Git, Bender, embgen
  • AMD Vitis / Vivado (for FPGA and RPU workflows)
  • Apptainer (for Yocto-in-container workflows)
  • CERN HoG (pulled as a submodule in FPGA projects)

The guide snippets need your own project repositories and tool paths. Complete workflow examples will be published in separate repositories.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
From the repository root:

uv sync

That installs Maestro, its Python dependencies, and the development tools.

docs.title: Minimal script
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path

from maestro.commands import BenderCommands, GitCommands, VitisCommands
from maestro.logging import setup_logging
from maestro.models import CommandConfig

log = setup_logging()

project_dir = Path("project")
git = GitCommands()
repo = git.clone("git@example.com:group/project.git", project_dir)

bender = BenderCommands(CommandConfig(cwd=repo.path))
bender.update()

vitis = VitisCommands()
vitis.run_python_script(VitisCommands.get_builtin("rpu_build"))

Every command wrapper runs subprocesses in a configured working directory, captures stdout/stderr, raises CommandError on failure (unless configured otherwise), and appends command output under the current Maestro run directory.

docs.title: Use the CLI
docs.text:
The same wrappers are available from the shell:

uv run maestro --help
uv run maestro --cwd project git sha --short

See CLI for how Python signatures map to flags.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Optional YAML next to where you invoke the script:

File Purpose maestro.yml Shared project defaults (committed) maestro.local.yml Machine-specific overrides (gitignored)

Copy maestro.local.yml.example to maestro.local.yml for local overrides. See Configuration and, for running commands in containers, Executors.

docs.title: Browse these docs locally
docs.text:
make docs_serve

Or build once with make docs_build.

docs.title: GitLab CI/CD Pipeline
docs.text:
Maestro's own checks run in GitHub Actions. This guide is for downstream FPGA projects hosted on GitLab.

To set up a GitLab CI/CD pipeline, you need:

  • A runner: a machine to execute your jobs
  • An environment: e.g. docker image
  • A pipeline configuration: .gitlab-ci.yml

Below some explanations to get started with CI/CD for a Xilinx FPGA project.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: See https://docs.gitlab.com/runner/install/linux-repository/ to install on your machine

docs.title: Register project
docs.text:
On GitLab go to CI/CD settings and register new runner. On the machine execute the provided snippet Preferably using docker.

Additional configuration for custom docker. In the config.toml of the GitLab runner on the machine 

concurrent = 4
check_interval = 0
connection_max_age = "15m0s"
shutdown_timeout = 0

[session_server]
  session_timeout = 1800

[[runners]]
  name = ...
  url = ...
  token = ...
  executor = "docker"
  environment = ["GIT_CONFIG_COUNT=1", "GIT_CONFIG_KEY_0=safe.directory", "GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0=*"]
  [runners.cache]
    Type = "local"
    Path = "/cache"
    Shared = true
    MaxUploadedArchiveSize = 0
  [runners.docker]
    tls_verify = false
    image = ...
    memory = "16g"                                                    # update memory
    privileged = false
    disable_entrypoint_overwrite = false                              # disable entrypoint overwrite
    oom_kill_disable = false
    disable_cache = false
    volumes = ["/cache"]
    cache_dir = "/cache"
    allowed_pull_policies = ["always", "if-not-present"]              # set pull policy for local images
    shm_size = 0
    network_mtu = 0

docs.title: GitLab Pipeline with custom image
docs.text:
Generate an image containing all dependencies including Xilinx Vitis, yocto deps and so forth. Create a cli script to build everything and use it in the pipeline.

Adapt the image, project names, and inv tasks to your workflow. See templates/gitlab-ci.yml as an example.

For custom local images set 

default:
  image:
    name: vitis_tools_user:2025.2
    pull_policy: if-not-present # available: always, if-not-present
    entrypoint: [""]

For pulling private repositories set, this configures the CI_JOB_TOKEN to be used with https git requests. 

  before_script:
    - |
      echo "
      machine $CI_SERVER_HOST
      login gitlab-ci-token
      password $CI_JOB_TOKEN
      " > ~/.netrc

docs.title: GitLab CI configuration
docs.text:
For HoG and other systems relying on full git history set under CI/CD > General pipelines

  • git strategy: git clone
  • git shallow clone: 0
  • timeout: at least 2h

See the HoG pipeline configuration guide for more details.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Maestro splits "what to run" from "how to run it".

flowchart LR
  yaml["maestro.yml / maestro.local.yml"] --> cfg["config_global"]
  script["workflow script"] --> cmds["commands.*"]
  cli["maestro CLI"] --> cmds
  cfg --> cmds
  cfg --> factory["Executor.factory"]
  factory --> exec
  cmds --> exec["executors.*"]
  exec --> sub["subprocess"]
  cmds --> logs[".maestro/runs/.../logs"]
  assets["assets: yocto.def, Vitis RPU, TCL"] --> cmds

docs.title: Config
docs.text: Importing maestro.config_global (or calling setup_logging) loads dataclass defaults, then maestro.yml, then maestro.local.yml from the invocation directory. Derived paths live under .maestro/ (runs, caches).

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Classes such as GitCommands and HoGCommands subclass Commands. They own a CommandConfig (cwd, env, isolation and silence flags) and an Executor. Public methods build argv lists and call self.run(...), which delegates to the executor and writes a per-tool log file for the run.

The executor is executor= if one is passed. Otherwise it is built from the id bound to the command in maestro.yml (executor_id= overrides the binding). See Executors.

docs.title: Executors
docs.text:
Executors start the actual process:

Executor Role BaseExecutor Host process (default) UVExecutor Prefix with uv run (typical for embgen) DockerExecutor Run in a Docker image, with bind mounts ApptainerExecutor Build/run a SIF from a .def, with bind mounts BashExecutor / PrefixExecutor Shell or fixed argv prefix

Swap executors on a command instance without changing the high-level API. For example, pass an ApptainerExecutor into YoctoCommands to run Yocto in a container, or use UVExecutor with EmbGenCommands.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text: maestro (also meastro, mao) discovers every *Commands class and builds maestro <tool> <method> --arg ... subcommands from signatures and docstrings. See CLI.

docs.title: Assets
docs.text:
Packaged helpers under maestro.assets:

  • Apptainer definition: apptainer_def("yocto")
  • Vitis RPU scripts: VitisCommands.get_builtin("rpu_setup" | "rpu_create" | "rpu_build")
  • Vivado TCL helpers used by VitisCommands (program, JTAG AXI, IP packaging)

docs.title: Typical call pattern
docs.text:
1. setup_logging()
  2. Construct command wrappers with CommandConfig(cwd=...) when needed
  3. Optionally .configure(...) an executor and pass it as executor=, or bind one in maestro.yml
  4. Call wrapper methods; inspect CommandResult or collected artifacts

Tool-specific environment variables (RPU_*, VITIS_*, RAUC_*, ...) are set in the workflow script via os.environ, not via Maestro YAML.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Configuration loads when maestro.config_global is imported. By default Maestro reads from the invocation directory (current working directory), unless you pass a path to load_config().

from pathlib import Path

from maestro.config_global import load_config

cfg = load_config(Path("/path/to/project"))

docs.title: Sources and override order
docs.text:
Later sources win:

  1. Dataclass defaults in Config
  2. maestro.yml
  3. maestro.local.yml
File Purpose maestro.yml Shared project defaults (committed) maestro.local.yml Machine-specific overrides (gitignored)

Copy maestro.local.yml.example to maestro.local.yml for local overrides.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text: Field Default Notes paths.root .maestro Root directory for Maestro-generated state log.level INFO Console and root logger level log.subdir logs Log directory inside each run directory log.format %(name)s: %(message)s Console format log.format_file %(asctime)s %(name)s %(levelname)s - %(message)s File format log.datefmt [%X] Console date format log.datefmt_file [%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S] File date format apptainer.cache_subdir apptainer Under paths.cache_dir yocto.cache_subdir yocto Under paths.cache_dir executors {} Named executor definitions, see Executors commands {} Per-command executor binding and options (e.g. yocto.yocto_workdir)

docs.title: Layout on disk
docs.text:
<invocation_dir>/<paths.root>/
  runs/<timestamp>/<log.subdir>/   # maestro.log + per-command logs
  cache/apptainer/                 # built .sif images
  cache/yocto/                     # optional download/sstate binds

Derived helpers on Config:

  • paths.root_dir, paths.run_dir, paths.cache_dir
  • log_dir, apptainer_cache_dir, yocto_cache_dir

docs.title: Example YAML
docs.text:
maestro.yml:

paths:
  root: .maestro

log:
  level: INFO

maestro.local.yml:

log:
  level: DEBUG

executors:
  yocto_env:
    type: apptainer
    def_file: yocto
    workdir_host: yocto

commands:
  yocto:
    executor: yocto_env
    yocto_workdir: yocto/2025.2

maestro.local.yml is deep-merged over maestro.yml. Lists are replaced, not appended.

Subprocess environment variables (Vitis/RPU/RAUC, ...) are not part of these files. Set them in the workflow script, or per command with CommandConfig(env={...}). That dict is merged over the host environment, and with isolated=True it replaces the host environment, including PATH.

docs.title: Executors
docs.text:
An executor decides where a command runs: on the host, through uv run, or inside a Docker or Apptainer container. Command wrappers stay the same. Only the executor changes.

Type Class Options default / base / - BaseExecutor none: host shell uv UVExecutor none: prefixes uv run bash BashExecutor none: runs through bash -c prefix PrefixExecutor prefix docker DockerExecutor image, workdir_host, workdir_container, binds, cli apptainer ApptainerExecutor def_file, workdir_host, workdir_container, binds

docs.title: Choosing an executor
docs.text:
Highest priority first:

  1. executor= passed to the command constructor (an executor instance)
  2. executor_id= passed to the command constructor (an id from maestro.yml)
  3. The binding under commands.<name> in maestro.yml / maestro.local.yml
  4. default (BaseExecutor)

docs.title: In code
docs.text:
from maestro.commands import EmbGenCommands
from maestro.executors import UVExecutor

embgen = EmbGenCommands(executor=UVExecutor())

docs.title: In YAML
docs.text:
executors:
  vitis_env:            # full definition: type + options
    type: docker
    image: vitis:2025.2
    workdir_host: .
    workdir_container: /workspace
    binds:
      - [../cache, /cache, rw]
  yocto_env:
    type: apptainer
    def_file: yocto     # built-in definition, or a path to a .def file
    workdir_host: yocto
  hog_exe: vitis_env    # alias of another id
  py: uv                # shortcut for {type: uv}
  host: default         # explicit host executor

commands:
  vitis: vitis_env      # short form
  hog: hog_exe
  embgen:
    executor: py        # long form, leaves room for per-command options
  yocto:
    executor: yocto_env
    yocto_workdir: yocto/2025.2

With this config, HoGCommands() runs in the Docker container without any code change, and so does maestro hog ... from the CLI.

docs.title: Resolution rules
docs.text:
• A string value is an alias if it names another executor id. Otherwise it is a type shortcut (py: uv is the same as py: {type: uv}).
  • default, base and - always mean BaseExecutor, even if no id is defined
  • Alias cycles (a: b, b: a) raise ValueError
  • Options are passed to the executor's configure() (or __init__ if it has no configure()). Unknown options and missing required ones raise ValueError.
  • An unknown id raises KeyError. An unknown type raises ValueError that lists the known types.
  • maestro.local.yml is deep-merged over maestro.yml. A list (such as binds) is replaced, not appended, so repeat the full list in the local file.

Executor types are discovered automatically: any *Executor class in maestro.executors can be used as a type:.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
Call setup_logging() once at the start of a workflow script.

from maestro.logging import setup_logging

log = setup_logging()
log.info("starting workflow")

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
1. Reads log.* settings from the loaded configuration
  2. Creates the run directory's log folder
  3. Attaches a Rich console handler (writing to stderr) and a file handler writing maestro.log
  4. Replays records logged before the call (they are buffered) onto both handlers

Because the console goes to stderr, stdout stays free for results. The CLI relies on this. If setup_logging() is never called, warnings and errors still reach stderr through a fallback handler.

Logger hierarchy uses the maestro root. Command wrappers add children such as maestro.cmd.git and maestro.cmd.hog.

docs.title: Command logs
docs.text:
Each Commands.run(...) appends argv and captured lines to:

.maestro/runs/<timestamp>/logs/<commandname>.log

for example git.log, hog.log, yocto.log. These files are always written. Console noise can be reduced through CommandConfig:

Flag Effect on the console silent=True Hide the command's output lines. The command line and errors are still logged. suppress=True Log nothing at all for the command

Pass a CommandConfig as the wrapper's default, or as cfg= to run(...) for a single call.

docs.title: Levels
docs.text: log.level controls the console and root logger (default INFO). The run file handler always records at DEBUG so a quiet console still leaves a detailed trace on disk.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Complete workflow examples will live in separate repositories. Links will be added here once those repositories are published.

For now, see Getting started and the workflow guides for register generation, Vivado and HoG, RPU firmware, and Yocto and Apptainer.

docs.title: Register generation
docs.text: Generate HDL, software, simulation, and Markdown register artifacts with EmbGenCommands, typically through UVExecutor so embgen runs via uv.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Git access to the hardware repo
  • embgen available to uv (Maestro already depends on it)

docs.title: Pattern
docs.text:
Replace the example repository URL with your hardware repository and adapt the YAML and output paths to its layout.

from pathlib import Path

from maestro.commands import EmbGenCommands, GitCommands
from maestro.executors import UVExecutor
from maestro.logging import setup_logging
from maestro.models import CommandConfig

log = setup_logging()
root = Path("project")

git = GitCommands()
git.clone("git@example.com:your-group/axis_windowing.git", root)

embgen = EmbGenCommands(CommandConfig(cwd=root), executor=UVExecutor())
yml = root / "sources" / "embgen" / "axis_windowing.yml"

embgen.generate(yml, ["hjson"], root / "sources/hdl/regs")
embgen.generate(yml, ["h", "py"], root / "sources/sw/regs")
embgen.generate(yml, ["md"], root / "docs")

generate takes an embgen YAML config, a list of target flags (hjson, h, py, md, ...), and an output directory.

docs.title: RPU firmware
docs.text: Build RPU applications with Bender dependencies and Maestro's built-in Vitis Python scripts (rpu_setup, rpu_create, rpu_build).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Vitis on PATH
  • An exported hardware XSA (e.g. from the Vivado / HoG step)
  • Git + Bender

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
The built-in scripts read process environment, not maestro.yml. Set them in the workflow before calling Vitis:

Variable Role RPU_ROOT_DIR Firmware project root RPU_XSA_FILE Path to the XSA RPU_DOMAIN_LIBRARIES Colon-separated domain libraries RPU_APP_NAME Application name RPU_APP_SOURCES Colon-separated source globs / paths

docs.title: Pattern
docs.text:
import os
from pathlib import Path

from maestro.commands import BenderCommands, GitCommands, VitisCommands
from maestro.logging import setup_logging
from maestro.models import CommandConfig

log = setup_logging()
root = Path("rpu_firmware")

os.environ["RPU_ROOT_DIR"] = root.as_posix()
os.environ["RPU_XSA_FILE"] = (root / "hardware/design.xsa").as_posix()
os.environ["RPU_APP_NAME"] = "test_app"
# ... other RPU_* ...

git = GitCommands()
bender = BenderCommands(CommandConfig(cwd=root))
vitis = VitisCommands()

bender.update()
vitis.run_python_script(VitisCommands.get_builtin("rpu_setup"))
vitis.run_python_script(VitisCommands.get_builtin("rpu_create"))
vitis.run_python_script(VitisCommands.get_builtin("rpu_build"))

VitisCommands.get_builtin(name) resolves scripts shipped under maestro.assets.vitis.

docs.title: Vivado and HoG
docs.text: FPGA flows use Bender for dependency scripts and CERN HoG (./Hog/Do) for project create and workflow. Maestro wraps both.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Vivado on PATH (or your site's module//usr/pack setup)
  • Git, Bender, HoG as a submodule of the hardware project

docs.title: Pattern
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path

from maestro.commands import BenderCommands, GitCommands, HoGCommands
from maestro.logging import setup_logging
from maestro.models import CommandConfig

log = setup_logging()
root = Path("vivado")

git = GitCommands()
git.clone("git@example.com:group/vivado.git", root, submodule_update=True)

bender = BenderCommands(CommandConfig(cwd=root))
hog = HoGCommands(CommandConfig(cwd=root))

bender.update()
bender.script("flist", root / "Top/vivado/proj/list/bender.src")

hog.create("vivado/proj")
hog.workflow("vivado/proj")

bits = hog.get_output_files("vivado/proj", "*.bit")
xsas = hog.get_output_files("vivado/proj", "*.xsa")

get_describe / get_output_files resolve HoG's bin/<group>/<project>-<describe>/ layout so you can copy bitstreams and XSAs into a shared folder for later stages.

Pass recreate=True to workflow to rebuild an existing project from scratch (HoG -recreate). From the shell: maestro --cwd vivado hog workflow --project vivado/proj --recreate.

docs.title: Yocto and Apptainer
docs.text: Yocto builds run inside an Apptainer image built from Maestro's built-in yocto.def. ApptainerExecutor builds/caches the SIF and remaps host paths; YoctoCommands runs repo and source setupsdk && ... in that environment.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Apptainer
  • For full Kria builds: an XSA and RPU ELF, plus binds for site tools (e.g. /usr/pack and PetaLinux/Vitis pack paths)

docs.title: Smoke test
docs.text:
A minimal script that only checks that the container runs:

from pathlib import Path

from maestro.commands import Commands
from maestro.executors import ApptainerExecutor, apptainer_def
from maestro.logging import setup_logging
from maestro.models import CommandConfig

log = setup_logging()
root = Path(__file__).parent

apptainer = ApptainerExecutor().configure(
    def_file=apptainer_def("yocto"),
    workdir_host=root,
)
commands = Commands(CommandConfig(cwd=root), executor=apptainer)
commands.run("ls", "-lah")

apptainer_def("yocto") finds the packaged definition. The SIF is cached under .maestro/cache/apptainer/yocto.sif (see Configuration).

docs.title: Full Yocto workflow
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path

from maestro.config_global import global_config
from maestro.commands import YoctoCommands
from maestro.executors import ApptainerExecutor, apptainer_def

root = Path("yocto")
cache = global_config.yocto_cache_dir

apptainer = ApptainerExecutor().configure(
    def_file=apptainer_def("yocto"),
    workdir_host=root,
    binds=[
        (Path("/usr/pack"), Path("/usr/pack"), "ro"),
        (
            cache / "build" / "downloads",
            Path("/workspace/yocto/2025.2/build/downloads"),
            "rw",
        ),
        (
            cache / "build" / "sstate-cache",
            Path("/workspace/yocto/2025.2/build/sstate-cache"),
            "rw",
        ),
    ],
)

yocto = YoctoCommands(yocto_workdir=root / "yocto/2025.2", executor=apptainer)
yocto.repo_init()
yocto.bitbake("petalinux-image-minimal")

Bind mounts keep downloads and sstate on the host cache while the container workdir maps to /workspace. bitbake(target) is shorthand for run_environment(f"bitbake {target}"), which runs after sourcing setupsdk.

docs.title: Configure in maestro.yml instead
docs.text:
You can declare the executor and work directory in YAML instead of building them in code:

executors:
  yocto_env:
    type: apptainer
    def_file: yocto
    workdir_host: yocto
    binds:
      - [/usr/pack, /usr/pack, ro]

commands:
  yocto:
    executor: yocto_env
    yocto_workdir: yocto/2025.2

YoctoCommands() then needs no arguments, and the CLI works the same way:

uv run maestro yocto bitbake --target petalinux-image-minimal

See Executors.

Build an executor from config (default, aliases, or type + options).

The maestro.yml should be of the format

executors:
    vitis_env:
        type: docker
        image: vitis:2025.2
        ...
        binds:
            - [../cache, /cache, rw]
    hog_exe: vitis_env    # alias
    some_exe_id: default  # executor_id can be defined, but use default exe

commands:
    uv: some_exe_id       # assign an executor_id
    git: default          # directly use default
    vitis: vitis_env      #
    hog: hog_exe          # use alias executor_id

docs.title: maestro.discover.discover_classes
docs.text:
discover_classes(
    package, suffix, cls, skip_modules=frozenset()
)

Generates a mapping short names to classes with a given suffix within a package.

Walks immediate submodules of package (via pkgutil.iter_modules), imports each one, and collects types whose names end with suffix and that are defined in that module (not re-exported imports). Protocol classes and private modules (names starting with _) are skipped.

Short names are derived by lowercasing the class name and stripping suffix (case-insensitive), e.g. GitCommands with suffix "Commands" yields "git".

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default package ModuleType

Package module whose submodules are scanned (must have __path__).

required suffix str

Class-name suffix to match (e.g. "Commands", "Executor").

required cls type[T]

Base type used to parameterize the returned class map.

required skip_modules frozenset[str] | set[str]

Submodule names to ignore during discovery.

frozenset()

Returns:

Type Description dict[str, type[T]]

Mapping from short name to discovered class.

Examples:

>>> from maestro import commands
>>> from maestro.commands.base import Commands
>>> discover_classes(commands, "Commands", Commands)
{'git': <class 'maestro.commands.git.GitCommands'>, ...}
